scenes.script_line: Every builder knows the importance of a foundation. But a landscape has a foundation too: living soil. It supports roots, stores water and contains organisms that recycle nutrients. When we damage soil, we may affect things far beyond the surface. We would never carelessly destroy a building's foundation. Let's give the natural foundation the same respect.

shots.text: close-up of a bricklayer's hand laying a foundation stone
macro of dark living soil with visible roots and organic matter
medium shot of a foreman kneeling to examine soil before building
wide shot of a small structure's foundation beside untouched garden ground

must_not: office foundation plans on a screen

scenes.script_line: Press a sponge hard. Its spaces shrink. Repeated heavy machinery can do something similar to soil: compact it and reduce the space for air and water. The damage may be invisible at first. That's why approved routes matter. Saving a few metres with a shortcut is not always saving time. Sometimes it's creating a problem beneath our feet.

shots.text: close-up of a hand pressing a sponge to show compression
medium shot of a small wheelbarrow following a marked approved route
close-up of compacted soil contrasted with loose healthy soil
wide shot of a crew member walking the long marked route instead of a shortcut

scenes.script_line: On a building site, we cover materials to protect them. Nature uses covers too. Leaves, plants and mulch protect soil from direct rain and strong sun. So a patch of ground with leaves is not necessarily dirty. It may be functioning well. Clear what must be cleared for safe work. Protect what helps the land stay healthy.

shots.text: close-up of mulch and fallen leaves covering garden soil
medium shot of a gardener spreading protective mulch by hand
wide shot of a garden bed covered in natural leaf litter
close-up of a worker clearing only the marked path, leaving mulch beside it
shots.pexels: worker clearing marked path leaving mulch

scenes.script_line: A machine can clear a patch of ground in a morning. But rebuilding healthy soil and vegetation may take many seasons, sometimes much longer. That's a strange comparison: hours to disturb, years to recover. So before moving beyond the approved work area, ask a simple question. Do we really need to disturb this ground? Sometimes the best job is the damage avoided.

shots.text: wide shot of a cleared patch of ground beside an untouched garden area
medium shot of a foreman marking the approved work boundary with tape
close-up of new shoots growing back in a previously cleared area
close-up of a worker's hand hesitating over a tool before stepping past the boundary

scenes.script_line: You can see a wall growing course by course. But much of the work inside healthy soil is invisible. Roots extend. Fungi grow. Organisms break down leaves. Invisible doesn't mean unimportant. Think of the hidden wiring and pipes inside a building. We protect them because they make the building work. Soil life deserves thoughtful protection too.

shots.text: close-up of exposed pipes and wiring inside an unfinished wall
macro of soil with visible fungi threads and root hairs
medium shot of a crew member carefully covering protected soil with a tarp
wide shot of a brick wall rising course by course beside a protected garden bed
